source.edition: Textbook for Class XII Part I, Reprint 2026-27

chapter.name: Determinants
chapter.blurb: Determinants of square matrices up to order three with real entries: evaluating them by expansion along a row or column, using them to find the area of a triangle, minors and cofactors, the adjoint and inverse of a square matrix, and applying matrices and determinants to check the consistency of a system of linear equations and solve it by the matrix method.

scope_in.item: Know that a determinant is a number associated with every square matrix, written |A|, det A or Delta, read as 'determinant of A' (not modulus), and that only square matrices have determinants
Evaluate determinants of order 1 (|[a]| = a) and order 2 (a11 a22 - a21 a12), including entries with variables or trigonometric functions
Expand a 3 x 3 determinant along any row or column with signs (-1)^(i+j), knowing all six expansions give the same value, and choose the row or column with the most zeros
Use |A| = k^n |B| when A = kB for square matrices of order n
Find unknowns from determinant equations such as |[[3, x], [x, 1]]| = |[[3, 2], [4, 1]]|
Find the area of a triangle as (1/2)|det [[x1, y1, 1], [x2, y2, 1], [x3, y3, 1]]|, taking the absolute value
Use a zero area determinant for collinearity and for the equation of the line through two points; find an unknown coordinate from a given area using both signs
Find minors M_ij and cofactors A_ij = (-1)^(i+j) M_ij of elements of 2 x 2 and 3 x 3 determinants
Evaluate a determinant as the sum of products of the elements of a row or column with their cofactors, and know that elements of one row times cofactors of another row sum to zero
Find adj A as the transpose of the cofactor matrix, including the 2 x 2 shortcut (interchange a11 and a22, change the signs of a12 and a21)
Use A(adj A) = (adj A)A = |A| I (stated without proof) and verify it for given matrices
Classify a matrix as singular (|A| = 0) or non-singular (|A| != 0); use |AB| = |A||B|, |adj A| = |A|^(n-1), and that AB, BA are non-singular when A, B are
Know A is invertible if and only if it is non-singular, and find A^(-1) = (1/|A|) adj A for 2 x 2 and 3 x 3 matrices
Find A^(-1) from a given matrix polynomial equation such as A^2 - 4A + I = O by multiplying by A^(-1)
Define consistent and inconsistent systems; decide consistency using |A| and (adj A)B
Write a system of linear equations in two or three variables as AX = B and solve it by the matrix method X = A^(-1)B, including simple word problems

scope_out.item: Properties of determinants (interchanging rows changes the sign, identical rows give zero, taking a common factor out of a row, adding a multiple of one row to another, |A^T| = |A|) and proofs by row/column operations
scope_out.reason: This rationalised edition has no Properties of Determinants section: the section list runs 4.1 Introduction, 4.2 Determinant, 4.3 Area of a Triangle (p. 82), so the old properties section is gone. Only vestigial references survive (the introduction on p. 76, a stray 'Using properties of determinants in Exercises 11 to 15' line on p. 100 with no such exercises, and an empty 'satisfy following properties' line in the Summary on p. 101). The only scaling fact taught is |kB| = k^n |B| (p. 80).

scope_out.item: Cramer's rule for solving linear systems
scope_out.reason: Not taught anywhere in the chapter; the only solution method is the matrix method X = A^(-1)B (pp. 94-99).

scope_out.item: Determinants of order 4 or higher, or with complex entries
scope_out.reason: The book states it studies determinants 'up to order three only with real entries' (p. 76).

scope_out.item: Finding the general solution of a system with infinitely many solutions
scope_out.reason: The book restricts itself to systems with unique solutions (Note, p. 94); for |A| = 0 and (adj A)B = O it only says the system may be consistent or inconsistent (p. 95).

scope_out.item: Inverse of a matrix by elementary row or column operations, and rank of a matrix
scope_out.reason: Not in this chapter; the inverse is found only through the adjoint (pp. 90-93) or a given matrix equation.

scope_out.item: Proofs of A(adj A) = |A| I, |AB| = |A||B| or the non-singularity of AB in general; the Cayley-Hamilton theorem by name
scope_out.reason: Theorems 1-3 are stated without proof (pp. 88-89); matrix equations like A^2 - 4A + I = O are given and verified, never derived from a named theorem (pp. 92-93).

scope_out.item: Area of a quadrilateral or polygon using determinants

concepts.name: Determinant of a matrix of order one and two
concepts.description: The determinant as a number associated with every square matrix, the notation |A| or det A, and evaluating determinants of order 1 and order 2, including finding an unknown entry from a determinant equation.
concepts.idea: Every square matrix has a single number attached to it called its determinant, written |A| or det A; |A| is read as 'determinant of A', not 'modulus of A', and only square matrices have determinants.
concepts.rule: For A = [a], |A| = a. For A = [[a11, a12], [a21, a22]], |A| = a11 a22 - a21 a12 (product of the leading diagonal minus product of the other diagonal).

concepts.name: Determinant of order three by expansion; |kA| = k^n |A|
concepts.description: Evaluating a 3 x 3 determinant by expanding along any row or column with the sign (-1)^(i+j), choosing the row or column with most zeros, and the scaling rule |kB| = k^n |B| for a matrix of order n.
concepts.idea: A 3 x 3 determinant is broken into three 2 x 2 determinants: each element of the chosen row or column is multiplied by its sign (-1)^(i+j) and by the 2 x 2 determinant left after deleting its row and column. All six expansions give the same value.
concepts.rule: Along R1: |A| = a11(a22 a33 - a23 a32) - a12(a21 a33 - a23 a31) + a13(a21 a32 - a22 a31). Signs follow the pattern + - + / - + - / + - +. If A = kB for square matrices of order n, then |A| = k^n |B|.

concepts.name: Area of a triangle using determinants
concepts.description: Writing the area of a triangle with given vertices as half the absolute value of a 3 x 3 determinant, using a zero value to test collinearity and find the equation of a line, and finding an unknown coordinate when the area is given.
concepts.idea: The coordinate formula for the area of a triangle is exactly half of a 3 x 3 determinant whose rows are (x, y, 1) for each vertex. Area is positive, so take the absolute value; collinear points give zero.
concepts.rule: Area = (1/2) |det [[x1, y1, 1], [x2, y2, 1], [x3, y3, 1]]|. If the area is given, use both the positive and negative values of the determinant. Three points are collinear exactly when this determinant is 0.

concepts.name: Minors and cofactors
concepts.description: Finding the minor M_ij and cofactor A_ij of an element, expanding a determinant as the sum of elements of a row or column times their cofactors, and the fact that elements of one row times cofactors of a different row sum to zero.
concepts.idea: The minor of an element is the smaller determinant left after deleting that element's row and column; the cofactor is the minor with the sign (-1)^(i+j) attached.
concepts.rule: A_ij = (-1)^(i+j) M_ij. |A| = a11 A11 + a12 A12 + a13 A13 (any row or column with its own cofactors). Elements of one row (or column) times the cofactors of a different row (or column) sum to 0.

questions.a: A21 = -(2 x 1 - 1 x 0) = -2; A22 = 1 x 1 - 1 x 2 = -1; A23 = -(1 x 0 - 2 x 2) = 4. a11 A21 + a12 A22 + a13 A23 = 1(-2) + 2(-1) + 1(4) = 0. This is the elements of R1 multiplied by the cofactors of R2, which equals a determinant with R2 replaced by R1 - two identical rows - so it is 0.

concepts.name: Adjoint of a matrix, singular matrices and determinant results
concepts.description: Forming adj A as the transpose of the cofactor matrix (including the 2 x 2 shortcut), the result A(adj A) = (adj A)A = |A| I, singular and non-singular matrices, |AB| = |A||B| and |adj A| = |A|^(n-1).
concepts.idea: The adjoint collects all the cofactors of A, transposed, so that multiplying it with A gives |A| on the diagonal and 0 elsewhere; whether |A| is zero splits matrices into singular and non-singular.
concepts.rule: adj A = transpose of [A_ij]. A(adj A) = (adj A)A = |A| I. A is singular if |A| = 0 and non-singular if |A| != 0. |AB| = |A||B|. For order n, |adj A| = |A|^(n-1). For [[a, b], [c, d]], adj A = [[d, -b], [-c, a]].
concepts.example: A = [[2, 3], [1, 4]]: A11 = 4, A12 = -1, A21 = -3, A22 = 2, so adj A = [[4, -3], [-1, 2]] (swap the diagonal, change the signs of the other two).

concepts.name: Inverse of a matrix using the adjoint
concepts.description: The condition for a square matrix to be invertible, finding A^(-1) = (1/|A|) adj A for 2 x 2 and 3 x 3 matrices, results such as (AB)^(-1) = B^(-1) A^(-1) and det(A^(-1)) = 1/det A, and finding A^(-1) from a matrix equation such as A^2 - 4A + I = O.
concepts.idea: A square matrix has an inverse exactly when it is non-singular; then dividing the adjoint by the determinant gives the inverse, because A(adj A) = |A| I.
concepts.rule: A is invertible if and only if |A| != 0, and then A^(-1) = (1/|A|) adj A. (AB)^(-1) = B^(-1) A^(-1), (A^(-1))^(-1) = A, det(A^(-1)) = 1/det(A). If A^2 + aA + bI = O with |A| != 0, multiply by A^(-1) to express A^(-1) in terms of A and I.

concepts.name: Consistency of linear systems and the matrix method
concepts.description: Writing a system of linear equations in two or three variables as AX = B, deciding consistency from |A| and (adj A)B, and solving a system with a unique solution by X = A^(-1)B, including simple word problems.
concepts.idea: A system of linear equations is one matrix equation AX = B; when the coefficient matrix A is non-singular, premultiplying by A^(-1) gives the unique solution.
concepts.rule: If |A| != 0: unique solution X = A^(-1)B (consistent). If |A| = 0 and (adj A)B != O: no solution (inconsistent). If |A| = 0 and (adj A)B = O: the system may be consistent or inconsistent.

questions.q: Solving AX = B with |A| = 0, a student writes: 'A^(-1) does not exist, so the system has no solution.' Evaluate this reasoning.
questions.a: Incomplete. When |A| = 0 the next step is to compute (adj A)B: if (adj A)B != O there is no solution, but if (adj A)B = O the system may still be consistent (for example x + y = 2, 2x + 2y = 4 has many solutions). The absence of A^(-1) alone does not decide it.
s: States that |A| = 0 alone does not decide consistency; (adj A)B must be checked
Notes that with (adj A)B = O the system may be consistent, ideally with an example
